In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), ambulatory BP predicts cardiovascular (CV) and kidney disease outcomes better than does office BP. 4-9 Similarly, nondipping status is associated with a poor CV and kidney prognosis in CKD patients. 4-6 Nonetheless, studies evaluating the prognosis of CKD patients based on ambulatory BP monitoring have focused on the role of nocturnal nondipping status and above-goal ambulatory BP independent of each other even though these 2 conditions are frequently associated. Indeed, current guidelines justify intensifying BP management in patients with above-goal ambulatory BP independent of the patient's nocturnal dipping status. Conversely, very little is known regarding the management of patients with nondipping status and ambulatory BP at goal. The decision as to whether such patients need to be treated requires as a first step more knowledge of the global risk associated with this phenotype.

Unfortunately, it remains unclear whether the presence of isolated nondipping status (ie, with ambulatory BP at goal) is associated with a different CV risk than that observed in CKD patients with ambulatory BP above goal

## PLAIN-LANGUAGE SUMMARY
Among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), ambulatory blood pressure (BP) monitoring improves the identification of individuals at high risk of clinical disease outcomes. Those with uncontrolled ambulatory BP are known to have a higher risk of developing cardiovascular disease and kidney disease progression, particularly when their ambulatory BP does not decline by at least 10% at night. Whether this is also true for patients with presence of optimal ambulatory BP levels but a BP pattern of no nighttime decline is largely unknown. We measured ambulatory BP in 900 Italian patients with CKD and followed them for several years. We found that, independent of ambulatory BP level, the absence of nighttime reductions in BP was associated with worsening of CKD and more frequent cardiovascular events. The absence of nighttime declines in BP is an independent risk factor for adverse events among patients with CKD. Futurestudies are needed to examine whether treating the absence of nighttime declines in BP improves clinical outcomes.

Similarly, the prognostic role of isolated nondipping status on kidney outcome has been investigated only rarely and was limited to CKD patients in Japan. 10,11 We previously demonstrated that switching administration of 1 antihypertensive drug from morning to evening in CKD patients with nondipping status and 24hour ambulatory BP at target is effective in restoring physiologic nocturnal BP decline. 12 This finding was not confirmed in Black individuals with hypertensive CKD. 13 However, no information on outcomes were provided in either study.

Therefore, we designed a prospective observational study to assess the prognostic effect of systolic ambulatory BP goal and dipping status, alone or in combination, on fatal and nonfatal CV events and kidney disease progression in a large cohort of patients with CKD who were not receiving dialysis.

## Outcomes
Co-primary outcomes were the occurrence of fatal and nonfatal CV events and a composite kidney disease

progression outcome. CV events included deaths due to CV causes certified by the National Death Registry and nonfatal events requiring hospitalizations due to myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, stroke, revascularization procedures, peripheral vascular disease, and nontraumatic amputation. For the CV survival analysis, follow-up was computed from the initial visit to December 2019 or the date of CV event, non-CV death, or first dialysis treatment. The kidney disease progression outcome was a composite of ≥ 50% eGFR decline or initiation of maintenance dialysis. Patients were followed until December 2019 or until the date of the kidney disease progression outcome or death, whichever occurred first.

## Survival Analysis: Kidney Disease Progression Outcome
We recorded 315 kidney disease progression events during a median follow-up period of 10.5 (IQR, 4.9-13.4) years, corresponding to a crude event rate of 4.94 (95% CI, 4.42-5.52) per 100 patient-years. Of these patients, 135

experienced an eGFR decline of ≥ 50%, and 180 initiated maintenance dialysis. The incidence rate of kidney disease progression events in the 4 groups is depicted in Figure 1B. The highest adjusted risk of this outcome was observed in patients with ambulatory BP above goal, with no difference by nocturnal dipping status ( P = 0.5). Among patients with ambulatory BP at goal, nondipping status was associated with 82% greater risk of the kidney disease progression outcome (Fig 2).

The isolated effect of ambulatory BP at goal and dipping status on the risk of the kidney disease progression outcome persisted when ambulatory BP at goal and dipping status were included separately (HRs of 1.66 [95% CI, 1.23-2.23] and 1.52 [95% CI, 1.15-2.02], respectively); in the model including both variables, ambulatory BP at goal (HR, 1.52 [95% CI, 1.12-2.07]) and dipping status (HR, 1.39 [95% CI, 1.04-1.86]) remained significantly associated with the kidney disease progression outcome.

In a sensitivity analysis, we defined the kidney disease progression outcome as initiation of maintenance dialysis; this outcome was recorded in 290 patients (180 without eGFR decline of ≥ 50% and 110 after detecting eGFR decline of ≥ 50%). The adjusted risk of dialysis initiation was 1.60 (95% CI, 1.01-2.54) in patients with ambulatory BP at goal and nondipping status; among patients with ambulatory BP above goal, the adjusted risk was 1.72 (95% CI, 1.02-2.90) and 2.19 (95% CI, 1.42-3.38) in those with dipping and nondipping status, respectively.
